2 Dan Sullivans In Alaska Senate Race Is Nothing New
Drama Behind 2 Dan Sullivans In Alaska’s Senate Race Becomes Major Legal Dispute, But This Ain’t New
Ok, even I can admit that the Tale of Two Dans — the debacle involving two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, both running for a U.S. Senate seat to represent Alaska — has become more of a saga than I expected, but it’s still much ado about nothing.
See, like many people, I figured Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, was simply being trolled by Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the island community of Petersburg, but, as we reported on Thursday, an investigation published by The New York Times strongly indicates Dan number 2 was actually a plant by the campaign of Dan number 1‘s Democratic opponent, Rep. Mary Peltola, who has denied any involvement in the so-called plot.
So, now, it’s become a whole Dan mess.
Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy responded to the Times story by ordering an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign for Senate should face criminal charges or civil penalties for allegedly scouring the state, looking for white guys named Dan Sullivan to confuse Alaskan voters. The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the Senate race, but only if the incumbent loses by a margin attributable to the alleged Peltola plot; according to CNBC, a federal judge is now fast-tracking motions by the campaign to dismiss the DOJ’s suit.
“The U.S. Constitution leaves the regulation of federal elections exclusively to the States and to Congress, and DOJ has no statutory authority to bring this case,” the motion argues.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump — who seems to be keenly aware that if Republicans lose control of Congress come the midterms, his GOP sycophant-provided quasi-dictatorship is over — has been losing whatever is left of his mind over the race.
In a recent social media post, Trump claimed, “Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan.”
But, even if the Times story is true, was it illegal? Was it fraud? Was it even uncommon?
The answer to all of the above is no.
See, the Times did that annoying thing that legacy media outlets do, where they sensationalize a thing by making it seem like it’s something egregious and unprecedented, when actually it’s precedented AF.
In fact, the Times report even acknowledged, “Ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska.” But then it went on to say, “But this operation, which has not been reported before, reveals the lengths to which Democrats went to seek advantage in a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber.”
So, which is it? Did Democrats do something both parties have done in the past, even in Alaska, or did Alaska Democrats go to great “lengths” to gain an advantage?
Yeah — it’s definitely the former.
From CNN:
In 2024, Washington’s Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined in the gubernatorial primary race by two other Democratic hopefuls with the same name.
Was it a coincidence? More like an age-old election trick that’s come up again in this year’s tightly contested Alaska U.S. Senate race.
In Washington two years ago, a Republican activist had paid the other two Bob Fergusons to run in the hopes that their names on the ballot would confuse voters — an effort to weaken the attorney general’s candidacy. But the decoys ultimately dropped out after just a few days when the first Bob Ferguson, who went on to be elected governor, threatened legal action and publicly derided their candidacy as an “attack on our democracy.”
So, not only has this been done before, but it has been done as recently as two years ago by Republicans. Just because when they tried it in 2024, the ops punked out at the threat of legal action doesn’t mean this isn’t still simply a “it’s all fun until the rabbit has the gun” kind of situation.
Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University, told CNN that ballot stacking is “a time-honored tradition,” and while he said it’s “not a good practice,” the truth is “if trying to confuse voters was a crime, then every politician would be in jail.”
CNN also pointed out other ballot-stacking instances going back nearly a century, including the 1930 Nebraska Republican U.S. Senate primary, when incumbent George W. Norris almost dropped out because another George W. Norris, a grocery clerk, was on the same ballot.
So, yeah, this whole thing might be entertaining, but it’s no scandal. If anything, it’s just a result of MAGA Republicans turning U.S. politics into a circus of perpetual absurdity, and Democrats finally deciding to stoop to their level.
Anyway, get out and vote, y’all.

sources.text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion , while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
The dueling developments came days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”
Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the senator.
Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.”
The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.
The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a “substantial risk” that Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy “will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity.”
“To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary,” the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.
Attorneys for the state have argued that Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That’s the same way in which they appeared on the August open primary ballot.
They also have argued that the state’s ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.
Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
It’s highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
At a campaign event in Juneau late Thursday, Peltola began her speech by saying she wanted to “clear the air.”
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about,” Peltola said. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times’ reporting, that he’d ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.
Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party sued state elections officials Friday, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau, Alaska.

sources.news_title: The Truth About the Alaska Dan Sullivan Shenanigans
sources.text:
Sign up for Executive Dysfunction, a weekly newsletter that highlights one under-the-radar story about how Trump is changing the law—or how the law is pushing back—and keeps you posted on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team.
Earlier this week, the New York Times published a splashy feature detailing how allies of Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee in this year’s Senate race in Alaska, worked to “stack” the ballot with candidates who could help her defeat the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan. As a result of these efforts, when Alaskans go to the polls next week, appearing alongside Peltola and Sullivan on the ballot will be one Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who voted for Peltola in previous elections—and who, according to the Times, was recruited by Democratic-operative types to play the spoiler role.
The Times’ implicit framing of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy as an election-swinging dirty trick requires a few caveats. First and most important, Alaska uses ranked choice voting, which means that Sen. Sullivan supporters confused by their two options can simply vote for both. Second, Peltola beat Sen. Sullivan by 8 points in the August primary, and Daniel J. Sullivan picked up 2.5 percent of the vote—significant, sure, but nowhere close to Peltola’s margin of victory. Third, Alaska officials have taken great pains to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot, displaying their names differently and designating Dan Sullivan as the incumbent.
Also, just speaking practically here, if you believed that the presence in a tightly contested Senate race of a person with the same name as a vulnerable incumbent in a tough year for Republicans was a complete coincidence, I have it on good authority that the bridge to nowhere is getting built after all, and I would sell it to you for a favorable price.
None of these facts have prevented President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans from getting very angry about this stunt. Before the Times story was published, Justice Department officials, at the president’s direction, had filed a lawsuit seeking to block state officials from certifying the results if Peltola beats Dan Sullivan by less than Daniel J. Sullivan’s share of the vote. (Again, thanks to ranked choice voting, this scenario is extremely farfetched, but stay with me.) After the Times story, Trump went much further, calling for criminal charges against Peltola and the “FAKE Dan Sullivan.” He also demanded that both of them be removed from the ballot, something that would give Republicans nervous about losing the Senate one fewer seat to worry about.
Sure enough, on Wednesday, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, announced that state officials were looking at “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws.” The DOJ, which had an eye on the race already, issued new subpoenas to Democrats linked to the non-senator Sullivan, whose candidacy Attorney General Todd Blanche described as “cheating” and “fraud.”
As is true of all breathless invocations of voter fraud by Republican politicians, however, Blanche’s claims do not hold up to scrutiny. The reality he is glossing over is that, as you would probably expect, there have already been legal challenges to Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, based in part on some of the details in the Times story. In June, though, an Alaska court determined that under state law, he has the same right to run for office as Sen. Sullivan or anyone else. What Peltola’s campaign (allegedly) did might be partisan skulduggery, but it is probably not illegal, and no one is getting kicked off the ballot or going to prison over it.
This case started back in May, when Daniel J. Sullivan filed to run for Senate as a Republican, despite never having previously been affiliated with the party. After the state GOP complained, the Alaska Division of Elections determined that under state law, Daniel J. Sullivan was ineligible to run because he had not filed “in good faith for the purpose of genuinely pursuing election” and had instead sought to “confuse or mislead” voters. The letter noted, for example, his request to be identified as “Dan,” like the incumbent. It also alluded to the subject matter of the Times story, highlighting his work with a political consultant who is a “known longtime supporter of Democratic candidates,” including Peltola.
Sullivan appealed, and in June, an Alaska trial court judge reversed the Division of Elections’ decision. The gist of Judge Thomas A. Matthews’ order, which the Alaska Supreme Court later affirmed, is that under state law, the qualifications to run for Senate straightforwardly track the language of the U.S. Constitution: Candidates must be at least 30 years old, have been citizens for at least nine years, and live in the state they seek to represent. Given that Daniel J. Sullivan checks all three boxes, Matthews found that officials had no authority to invent an additional “good faith” requirement and use it to “exclude an otherwise qualified candidate.”
Matthews’ opinion does not suggest that he is naive about what’s going on here. But critical to his analysis is the fact that under state law, the Division of Elections could have previously taken steps to prevent this from happening but didn’t: He points out that other states have dealt with same-name races, and that many have rules for weighing the “good faith” of prospective candidates. Since Alaska officials “could have predicted this situation would eventually arise,” Matthews concluded, they “may not now assert a new requirement, standard, limitation, or qualification after presentation of the candidate’s declaration.”
The attention generated by the Times story has Republicans looking to impose consequences that go well beyond the confines of Alaska election law. The challenge they face is that, as the Times acknowledged, ballot-stacking techniques are “common in politics,” are “generally considered legal,” and have been “employed by both parties in Alaska.” Peltola knows this better than most: In 2024, when she lost her bid for reelection to the House, Republicans went to court to ensure that Eric Hafner, who is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence in New York for threatening to kill judges, remained on the ballot as a Democrat. During the primary campaign in this very election, outside groups were pouring money into the state, hoping to sabotage Peltola by placing other Democrats on the general election ballot.
Intuitively, recruiting a candidate with the same name as another candidate feels like a more nefarious form of ballot stacking. But so far, Republicans’ efforts to draw a legal distinction have been vague, speculative, nonsensical, or some combination thereof. On Truth Social, for example, Trump claimed that the Times had revealed that Democrats had lied “under oath in Federal Court,” which is an accurate description of a crime, but not a thing that happened here. The Wall Street Journal reported that federal prosecutors are “exploring” whether to “bring charges alleging a conspiracy to violate voters’ rights.” There are real laws that protect these rights, but prosecutors generally use them to target people who threaten voters or try to trick them into not voting—for example, this guy, who in 2016 posted memes urging Hillary Clinton supporters to “vote” via text message. (Even that conviction was overturned on appeal.)
Whatever you think of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, it is not an illegal effort to stop people from voting: He is running for office, under his real name, in the state where he lives. Anyone who gets “tricked” into voting for him (and only for him) is still, in fact, voting. Even if one of the more ambitious Trump prosecutors decides to give it a shot, the First Amendment will present serious challenges, since going after candidates and their supporters for ostensibly harboring ulterior motives would criminalize a lot of things that parties in this country already do.
In context, the threats Republicans are issuing right now are best understood not as fully baked legal theories but as performances intended to convey to Trump that they, too, are angry about getting played and are looking into it very strongly. Dunleavy, Alaska’s governor, told the Wall Street Journal that he informed Trump that he is “investigating at the state level,” which is what I would tell the incensed leader of my party if I knew he wanted me to do something but there was little I could do and less than a week in which to do it.
The more likely (and more serious) implication of the story is the possibility of Trump and his allies using it as the basis of a new round of “stolen election” allegations. By loudly investigating the matter now, they are leaving open the possibility of challenging the results, not with oafish phone calls or a horde of Trump supporters storming the Capitol, but with the institutional power of the Justice Department. Citing unproven allegations to pressure Alaska officials not to certify a hypothetical Peltola victory—Dunleavy has said he is open to holding up the process, “depending upon the outcomes of this investigation”—feels like a long shot, but if control of the Senate comes down to Alaska, Trump is at least going to take it.
The one bit of good news here is that if this Alaska Public Media report is any indication, actual voters do not care all that much. One described the allegations as “nothing that we haven’t heard before.” Others expressed frustration with all the media focus on the ballot, rather than the policy positions of the people on it. Still others understandably took offense at the notion that Alaskans are not smart enough to figure out how to vote. This is shady business. But for better and for worse, in this country, “shady” is just how politics works.

The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings. I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The evidence will determine what happens next. Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support. Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.
— Governor Mike Dunleavy (@GovDunleavy) October 29, 2026
Multiple grand jury subpoenas will be issued in the coming days and preservation orders regarding text messages and emails are being prepared for cell phone companies to help build the case, sources told Fox News Wednesday.
Aides from the DSCC reportedly introduced Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz to former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios and former chief of staff Anton McParland. Kurtz reportedly traveled to Alaskan communities to recruit residents to run as Republicans. The other Sullivan, who supported Peltola’s candidacy, agreed to run.
Alaska’s open voting system made this scheme possible, given that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. Republicans backed an effort to help a candite serving time in a New York prison stay on the ballot when Peltola ran for reelection to the House in 2024.
Text messages showed that members of the DSCC and Peltola’s campaign considered creating a MAGA Party, although the plans never came to fruition, according to the Times.
Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement with either Sullivan’s campaigns. She is the only Democrat who will appear on the ballot.
The other Sullivan changed his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated Monday, eight days before the general election, according to the Alaska Beacon, a local outlet.
Democratic strategist Amber Lee authored a press release announcing the other Sullivan’s candidacy, metadata reviewed by the DCNF showed. Lee told The Hill in January that she believed there was a good chance Peltola could defeat Sullivan and previously hoped Peltola would run for governor.
Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher informed Sullivan in an Aug. 26 letter that his declaration of candidacy “was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy,” but rather to confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan. After Sullivan appealed the ruling, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled he could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary.
The Alaska Supreme Court overturned that ruling in a June 30 decision and allowed the other Sullivan to be on the ballot. The DSCC and Peltola’s campaign celebrated the high court’s decision, according to the Times.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Alaska voters will decide one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races on Tuesday as the Justice Department escalates a criminal investigation into whether one of the candidates was recruited to run by the campaign of another in an effort to confuse voters.
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces a strong challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola in his bid for a third term. Among the two other candidates to advance out of the Aug. 18 primary is a former teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting the challenger Daniel J. Sullivan, allegedly to siphon votes away from the incumbent Dan Sullivan in this marquee Senate race that could decide control of the chamber.
President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 23 before the Times story published that he ordered the Department of Justice to file suit to block certification of the election if Peltola wins. Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot.
Sen. Sullivan appears on ballots as “Dan S. Sullivan” alongside the labels of “Republican” and “Incumbent.” Challenger Sullivan is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without any party affiliation indicated, although he filed for office as a Republican.
State Republican Party officials had previously tried unsuccessfully to block Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the primary ballot, accusing him of colluding with Democrats to help elect Peltola. An Alaska court overturned efforts to boot the challenger from the primary ballot.
Alaska voters will also decide races for House, governor, state Legislature and two statewide ballot measures.
Although the state has a long history of favoring Republican candidates for federal office, this year marks the third consecutive election cycle in which Alaskans could swing the balance of power in Washington. Peltola has been on the ballot in each of those cycles.
Peltola placed first among 16 contenders in the state’s Aug. 18 all-party primary, in which the top four vote-getters advanced to the general election regardless of party affiliation. Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 8 p.m. local time, which is midnight and 1 a.m. ET. Almost all polls in the state close at midnight ET, but one polling location in the Aleutian Islands closes at 1 a.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners for Senate, House, governor, state Senate, state House and two statewide ballot measures.
How many people actually vote?
About 262,000 votes were cast in Alaska’s 2022 Senate election.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 35% of the vote in the 2022 Senate election was cast early in-person or by mail.

Alaska is expected to release a mix of in-person Election Day and early in-person voting results in its first vote update of the night. Typically, nearly all in-person Election Day results and in-person early voting results are released by the last update of the night, with the bulk of mail voting results released in the days following election night.

In the 2024 general election, the AP first reported results in Alaska at 1:07 a.m. ET, or seven minutes after the final polls closed. The vote count reached the halfway mark at about 2:07 a.m. ET. The last vote update of the night was at 7:15 a.m. ET Wednesday morning, with about 75% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
Recounts in Alaska are automatic in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request and pay for a recount. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Dan Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News.
The subpoenas are targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody involved in the race has been charged with a crime.
The department also amended its civil lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion," adding in details from a New York Times report on alleged efforts by people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from Sullivan. The new filing calls the situation a "conspiracy to undermine the integrity of the electoral process."
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel S. Sullivan has said in the past he is genuinely interested in running.
During a briefing with reporters Thursday, a Justice Department official offered perspective into the department's investigative approach in its criminal probe, saying there had been a "significant increase in activity" surrounding the Alaska race over the previous 24 hours. The Times report was published on Wednesday.
The Times' article detailed internal emails and text messages from individuals with knowledge of the alleged recruitment efforts — information the official suggested might significantly expand the government's ability to pursue its criminal investigation, since such communications are historically difficult for investigators to obtain without search warrants or voluntary cooperation from individuals with access to the material.
The official also alluded to possible investigative steps, like preservation requests to technology companies, search warrants for electronic communications and grand jury subpoenas seeking documents or testimony from those allegedly involved.
Asked what federal crimes could be implicated by an alleged recruitment scheme, the Justice Department official identified two civil rights statutes, 18 U.S.C. Sections 241 and 242, as potential roads for prosecutorial action.
Section 241 prohibits conspiracies to interfere with federally protected rights, including voting rights, while section 242 centers on willful deprivation of rights under color of law. The official added that prosecutors might, in a situation like this, examine whether there was a coordinated effort to trick voters into selecting a candidate.
The official referenced the federal prosecution of Douglass Mackey, convicted of conspiracy for posting misleading messages online during the 2016 election falsely encouraging Hillary Clinton supporters to vote by text message. That conviction was ultimately overturned by a federal appeals court in 2025.
Still, a Justice Department official acknowledged that the agency was not aware of any confirmed instances in which an Alaska voter had mistakenly cast a ballot for the wrong Dan Sullivan.

Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed a separate state investigation this week, ordering Alaska's Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law and whether criminal or civil action is merited.

sources.news_title: Justice Department reportedly issues new subpoenas over Alaska spoiler candidate controversy - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department is escalating a criminal investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Thursday.
Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.
More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the total number of them were immediately clear.
It’s the latest aggressive move by the Justice Department in a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
The information came to light the same day that the U.S. Justice Department issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration. Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
Race is among a handful that could determine control of the Senate
For months, the Justice Department has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
The new subpoenas were confirmed by a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe.
Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”
“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska’s Republican governor has also ordered an investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper’s reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. ”It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which The New York Times’ story alleges was involved in the effort to recruit the other Dan Sullivan, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation in Alaska isn’t that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK’d the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.”
AP writers Seung Min Kim, Nick Riccardi, and Ali Swenson contributed to this report.

The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska’s Republican Governor Has Also Ordered An Investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper’s reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Peltola Dismisses The Claims As A ‘Distraction’
Peltola alluded to the controversy in a fundraising post Thursday. “They can’t win on their record so they’re trying to intimidate me into backing down,” she said, adding later: “This is just another distraction as they avoid answering for the skyrocketing cost of living we’re facing because of their tariffs and forever wars. It won’t work.”
In Juneau, Alaska, independent Carter Bancroft said he voted Thursday for Peltola. “I’m very certain in the candidates I wanted to vote for and I wanted to vote for Mary Peltola,” he said.
But he said the latest claims have bothered him. He worries they give “ammunition” to Trump and others to attack Peltola or other Democratic candidates. “And I think I’m bothered by shenanigans on either side,” Bancroft said, especially actions intended “to confuse things or try to trick people.”
John Delgado, an independent who leans Republican, said he has “warmed up” to Sen. Sullivan, especially in light of the recent claims. He agrees that Peltola should drop out of the race.
The situation in Alaska isn’t that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court Ok’d The Other Sullivan On The Ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”

sources.news_title: Justice Department’s Dan Sullivan criminal probe accelerates after Alaska campaign revelations
sources.text:
The Justice Department has dramatically accelerated a criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate intended to siphon votes from the Republican, issuing dozens of new grand jury subpoenas and homing in on new potential charges, according to people familiar with the investigation.
The moves came on the heels of a New York Times report published Wednesday describing an alleged coordinated effort linked to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign. The report provided investigators material that they hadn’t previously obtained, two officials familiar with the matter said.
Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by that evening, one of the officials said.
Additional subpoenas are expected on Thursday, that person added.
The Alaska activity follows an already frenetic series of Justice Department actions that have marked a stark difference with previous administrations, including the first Trump term, when it took pains to remain out of the public eye in the weeks leading up to the election.
Justice Department officials claim the Alaska investigation, a highly-visible search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home, criminal charges against prominent critics of the president, grand jury subpoenas to California election officials and challenging voter rolls in several states, are normal and time-sensitive law enforcement activity.
They also frame the election-related efforts in Alaska and other states as intended to safeguard the votes, not sway the election as critics have alleged.
‘Decoy Dan’ and Alaskan voters
The federal investigation over Daniel J. Sullivan, nicknamed “Decoy Dan” by his opponents, had been moving at a slow clip, people familiar with the matter said.
Republican state officials had sought to disqualify the Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, arguing his was not a genuine candidacy but rather an attempt to confuse voters who wanted to vote for incumbent Sen. Daniel Sullivan. But the state supreme court rejected those efforts and restored the dueling Sullivans on the ballot.
Michael Heyman, the US Attorney in Alaska, recused himself early in the federal criminal investigation in part because he was in discussions with Senators Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski for a judgeship nomination in the state, sources familiar with the matter said. That left the investigation to be run by career officials in his office and prosecutors from the department’s Civil Rights Division.
The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks. A department official denied the alleged backlash.
Before Wednesday, prosecutors had issued some grand jury subpoenas and interviewed witnesses, one of the sources said, though at least one of the witnesses has largely gone quiet in recent months.
After the Times article published, some department officials questioned why the Times appeared to have evidence that prosecutors had not yet obtained.
Heymen un-recused Wednesday afternoon at the request of department leadership.
“Suddenly the options in the criminal case became much wider,” a department official said Thursday.
A second department official said investigators were looking to potentially bring civil rights charges, including a deprivation of rights charge that more typically is levied against law enforcement officials for wrongdoing.
“I think they should be prosecuted,” President Donald Trump said Wednesday, referring to Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.”
The lawsuit
Separately, department officials filed a long-shot lawsuit last week seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan loses and the votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan under the ranked choice system would have been enough to change the outcome.
Senior department attorneys worked quickly to amend that lawsuit, which proposes an undefined “investigation” into whether voters were misled, after the Times article was published.
In the new version of the federal lawsuit, the department alleges that the Peltola campaign and a national Democratic Party office submitted “misleading” arguments about their knowledge of the alleged efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan. To that point, it cites twelve different excerpts from the Times report.
“Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief,” the new lawsuit states. “It also aligns with common sense.”
Alaska’s Republican-led elections office is pressing a court to dismiss the case quickly, arguing that lawsuit seeks to sow “doubt” and will “cast a cloud over” the contest. Because of Alaska’s ranked-choice system, it could be weeks before the winner of the Senate race is declared.
Critics have slammed the lawsuit as political maneuvering, particularly after Trump told reporters he directed it. Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to walk back the assertion by saying in an interview days later that Justice Department was conducting its own research, but declined to discuss his conversations with Trump, who had publicly raised the issue for months.
State and federal officials briefly discussed a potential settlement in the case but have been unable to agree on what one source described as a “middle-of-the-road approach.” Among the proposals was providing additional instructions for poll workers to clarify for voters which Sullivan is which.
Some inside the department privately admit that the Alaska lawsuit, which is all but destined to fail, still serves a purpose by creating headlines that warn Alaskans about what one source described as a “massive voter fraud attempt.”
A state official told CNN that there are examples of voters who are well-informed about the dueling Sullivans still erroneously filling out their ballots and having to seek new ballots. It’s unclear how many of the spoiled ballots are related to the Sullivans confusion.
It’s a “preservation lawsuit” one federal official told CNN. “It will allow us to challenge the election if a challenge becomes necessary.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) have exchanged sharp accusations in an Alaska lawsuit involving alleged “voter confusion” in the U.S. Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and two men whose names are remarkably similar.

“Given a change in circumstances—the New York Times reporting that Proposed Intervenor Alaskans For Mary and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters—the United States withdraws its opposition to the Motion to Intervene,” the DOJ’s three-page notice states.
Although the report may be unwelcome news for Democrats, the DOJ’s filing places all sides in agreement over which parties should be allowed to litigate the case.
Earlier Wednesday, the Democratic Party pointed to an earlier filing in which the defendants “made clear that they do not oppose” intervention. That filing said it is “well-established that candidates and their campaigns have sufficient interest in election litigation to support intervention.”
“Defendants effectively acknowledge that they cannot adequately represent these intervenors’ unique interests,” the 11-page response says. “The partisan and electoral interests of Alaskans for Mary and DSCC in winning the election are fundamentally different in kind from State Defendants’ generalized interests in avoiding federal interference with the State’s management of Alaska’s election.”

The DSCC filing also draws attention to several differences between the arguments advanced by the Democratic groups and those presented by Alaska officials.
“Defendants do not significantly develop why the Purcell doctrine bars DOJ’s claim,” the response says. The doctrine reflects the principle that courts should be cautious about making major changes to state election rules shortly before an election.
“Defendants also do not explicitly argue that the Complaint fails to plausibly allege a risk of voter confusion,” the filing continues. “Moreover, unlike Alaskans for Mary and DSCC, State Defendants suggest DOJ’s claim may be ‘not yet ripe,’ with the implication that it may become ripe after the election. The government’s now-withdrawn opposition filing offered a different interpretation—one that Republicans may view as especially significant in light of the latest developments.
“With no apparent sense of irony, Proposed Intervenors decry ‘a nationwide attack on free elections’—in defense of including on the ballot a sham candidate whose sole reason for running is to mislead voters into accidentally voting for him, with the goal of assisting the Democrat,” the DOJ wrote in the defunct 13-page opposition filing.

DOJ issues new subpoenas in Alaska Senate race investigation over candidate recruitment
The Justice Department has begun issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal investigation into Alaska’s Senate race, including the alleged efforts by Democrats to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter confirmed to WTX US News.
The subpoenas are targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on Alaska’s ballot. Nobody involved in the race has been charged with a crime.
The department also amended its civil lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Sullivan loses due to “voter confusion,” adding in details from a New York Times report on alleged efforts by people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from Sullivan. The new filing calls the situation a “conspiracy to undermine the integrity of the electoral process.”
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel S. Sullivan has said in the past he is genuinely interested in running.
During a briefing with reporters Thursday, a Justice Department official offered perspective into the department’s investigative approach in its criminal probe, saying there had been a “significant increase in activity” surrounding the Alaska race over the previous 24 hours. The Times report was published on Wednesday.
The Times’ article detailed internal emails and text messages from individuals with knowledge of the alleged recruitment efforts — information the official suggested might significantly expand the government’s ability to pursue its criminal investigation, since such communications are historically difficult for investigators to obtain without search warrants or voluntary cooperation from individuals with access to the material.
The official also alluded to possible investigative steps, like preservation requests to technology companies, search warrants for electronic communications and grand jury subpoenas seeking documents or testimony from those allegedly involved.
Asked what federal crimes could be implicated by an alleged recruitment scheme, the Justice Department official identified two civil rights statutes, 18 U.S.C. Sections 241 and 242, as potential roads for prosecutorial action.
Section 241 prohibits conspiracies to interfere with federally protected rights, including voting rights, while section 242 centers on willful deprivation of rights under color of law. The official added that prosecutors might, in a situation like this, examine whether there was a coordinated effort to trick voters into selecting a candidate.
The official referenced the federal prosecution of Douglass Mackey, convicted of conspiracy for posting misleading messages online during the 2016 election falsely encouraging Hillary Clinton supporters to vote by text message. That conviction was ultimately overturned by a federal appeals court in 2025.
Still, a Justice Department official acknowledged that the agency was not aware of any confirmed instances in which an Alaska voter had mistakenly cast a ballot for the wrong Dan Sullivan.
“I think I’ve not heard of that, but it’s hard to tell exactly,” the official said when asked whether voters had reported confusion or attempted to correct their ballots.
Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed a separate state investigation this week, ordering Alaska’s Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law and whether criminal or civil action is merited.
WTX US News has reached out to the Department of Justice, Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment.
Separate civil lawsuit also expands
The criminal investigation is ramping up alongside a separate civil lawsuit filed by the Trump administration last week, seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election results under certain circumstances if the Republican incumbent loses.
That lawsuit addresses the government’s concerns that votes intended for Sen. Sullivan could instead go to Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whose candidacy was previously challenged by state election officials but ultimately greenlit by Alaska’s Supreme Court.
The suit, which argues Sullivan’s candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include the Times’ reporting. It now includes a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a “conspiracy.”
“Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief. It also aligns with common sense,” the amended complaint reads.
Alaska officials have previously asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that election administration is a state responsibility.
During Thursday’s briefing, before the suit was amended, Justice Department officials largely characterized the civil lawsuit as an effort to preserve the government’s ability to challenge an election result if deemed necessary.
“I don’t see this as much more than a preservation suit,” one official offered, arguing that once ballots are counted and separated from envelopes, establishing whether individual voters were confused becomes increasingly challenging.
The official also expressed interest in obtaining discovery concerning what Peltola’s campaign knew about the alleged recruitment operation, and furthermore, when campaign officials may have learned of it.
President Trump has railed against the Alaska ballot situation, calling for Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be taken off the ballot. Asked by reporters about the Justice Department’s lawsuit, he said last week: “Well, I’m the one that said, ‘Do it.'”

sources.news_title: Trump administration seeks to block Peltola Senate win in Alaska
sources.text:
The U.S. Department of Justice filed suit against the Alaska Division of Elections late Thursday, Oct. 22, seeking to block the division from certifying the result of the state's U.S. Senate election if the Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, wins.
President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday in Florida that he ordered the lawsuit be filed.
"I'm the one that said, 'do it,'" he said.
Peltola is the leading opponent to incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and polls show her with a small lead over Sullivan, but the race also includes two other people - Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer and undeclared candidate Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg.
In the complaint, the Department of Justice claims that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy is "frivolous," and was intended solely to confuse voters and benefit Peltola.
Until there is an investigation to determine the extent of that confusion, the Department of Justice argues, Alaska should not be permitted to certify the result of the ongoing Senate election.
Legal experts immediately dismissed the federal argument as bunk.
'A sad and scary sight'
Under the U.S. Constitution, states have authority over their own elections. The federal claim is based on the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act, which states in part that the law is intended "to protect the integrity of the electoral process."
In an immediate analysis posted online, Notre Dame Law School election law professor Derek Muller said, "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I've ever seen."
In addition to being poorly argued, it was poorly written, he said, noting that one paragraph is missing a verb that would ask the court to take action.
Libby Bakalar is a former Alaska state elections attorney who frequently speaks against the Trump administration. On social media Friday morning, she said the federal argument "is laughably bad, almost to the point of sanctionably frivolous. Watching MAGA on the ropes like this in court up here is a sad and scary sight."
The case has been referred to Judge Sharon Gleason, an Obama appointee who is the most senior of the two judges in the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.
Trump says he made the call to file the lawsuit
In numerous prior interviews, Dan J. Sullivan has said that his candidacy was motivated by dissatisfaction with Sen. Sullivan, and that he is not linked to the Democratic Party or Peltola's campaign.
Democratic officials have said the same thing.
But that hasn't stopped Trump and Sen. Sullivan - as well as other Republicans - from accusing both Peltola and Petersburg Sullivan of fraud.
Trump and other administration officials hinted throughout the summer and fall that they were working to bring a criminal case against Dan J. Sullivan, who was a registered Republican in July. He's now listed as "undeclared," an independent, in state voter files.
Thursday's filing does not name him as a defendant.
The listed attorneys for the Department of Justice are Stanley E. Woodward, an associate attorney general in Washington, D.C. and E. Bryan Wilson, an assistant U.S. attorney in Anchorage.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman was at Trump's rally in Wasilla this month.
"I told him - I just shook his hand, took a picture - I said I hope you're going to make sure there's no cheating, because any place you have rank(ed) choice, you have damn bad cheating. And we can't let that happen. So, we're going to defend the integrity of Alaska's elections," Trump said at the Oct. 13 event.
Legal action isn't expected until after the election
By phone, Muller said he doesn't expect the federal government's case to advance until after Election Day, if at all.
That's because the lawsuit is based on possible confusion by Dan J. Sullivan voters. If Dan S. Sullivan wins, any confusion didn't matter. If Peltola wins by a margin bigger than the number of votes for Dan S. Sullivan, the confusion wasn't decisive.
"The court's going to sit and wait till after the election to adjudicate it. Presumably, anyway," Muller said.
Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting, any hypothetical confused voter would simply have to rank both Sullivans to have their vote count the way they want.
"If there's any confusion, a lot of that is mitigated by ranked choice voting ... it's really not going to affect the outcome of the election simply because of the way ranked choice voting is designed to work," he said.
Even in a scenario where Judge Gleason declines to dismiss the case and Peltola wins by a smaller margin than the number of first-choice votes for Dan J. Sullivan, Muller said, the federal government would have to find those Dan J. Sullivan voters and prove they were confused.
"It's an impossible evidentiary question at the end of the day," he said.
Tom Lamb is a former Republican U.S. Senate candidate who argued in favor of Dan J. Sullivan in an Alaska Supreme Court case earlier this year. He's preparing to do so in the newly filed federal case too, and said there's no way to prove what the federal government wants to.
"If I say I voted for Sullivan Jr. and I made a mistake, there's no way of verifying that," he said.
Peltola or her campaign may intervene in suit
Reached by email Friday morning, Dan J. Sullivan declined immediate comment, saying the lawsuit came as a surprise and he was still analyzing it. He did not answer additional messages Friday seeking an interview.
The Beacon contacted the Division of Elections and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom early Friday and repeatedly throughout the day. Sam Curtis, a spokesman for the Department of Law, said Friday afternoon that the division is "focused on running the ongoing election and giving voters confidence that their votes will count."
The Department of Law represents the division and lieutenant governor in court.
"The complaint is being reviewed, and we do not have any comment on the litigation," he said.
A person affiliated with Sen. Sullivan's campaign said Friday morning that he did not ask the Department of Justice to file the lawsuit and that he was surprised by the act.
Nate Adams, campaign spokesman for Sullivan, said by email, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course. Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he'll keep building on for the next six years."
The chair of the Alaska Republican Party, Carmela Warfield, did not return a text message or phone call seeking comment Friday.
Harry Child, a spokesperson for Peltola's campaign, replied to questions by text message and implied that the campaign may intervene in the lawsuit.
"This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan's allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he'll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans' expense for over a decade," Child said. "We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections."
Asked his opinion, Alaska Democratic Party chair Eric Croft said, "Dan Sullivan is scared he'll lose and that's why he's looking to any corrupt, desperate method to win."
Review of primary election results indicates few voters were confused
Alaska's state courts have already argued - and decided - Dan J. Sullivan's eligibility as a candidate. In June, the Alaska Division of Elections struck him from the primary ballot, saying his candidacy was "for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters."
He appealed that decision, and in late June, an Anchorage Superior Court judge overturned the division's decision.
"The director's assertion that Mr. Sullivan seeks to confuse or misguide voters is not supported by a preponderance of evidence," wrote Judge Thomas Matthews in a 32-page analysis.
The state appealed, but the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the trial court's decision on June 29. It has not yet published a full explanation of its decision.
The state did not seek an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
After that decision, Peltola, Dan J. Sullivan, Dan S. Sullivan and 13 other candidates appeared on the primary ballot in August. Peltola finished first, with 49.5% of the vote, followed by Dan S. Sullivan with 41.4% and Dan J. Sullivan with 2.5%.
The fourth-place finisher, Democratic candidate David Leslie, withdrew from the election, an act that promoted Heikes into the final four with 1.1% of the vote.
A subsequent review of the results by the Anchorage Press found a large proportion of votes for Dan J. Sullivan came from left-leaning districts, indicating that Democratic-inclined voters - rather than confused Republicans - put the Petersburg man into the general election.
"I feel pretty vindicated that it seems to prove that there was very little, if any, voter confusion between the senator and myself," Dan J. Sullivan told local radio station KFSK-FM after the result.
The AlaskaBeacon.com is a donor-funded independent news organization in Alaska.
Different looks on the general election ballot
On the general election ballot, the two Sullivans are listed distinctively, as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.” The state’s Division of Elections does not list a party affiliation for the Petersburg Sullivan, and he is listed as an “undeclared” candidate, a kind of independent, in current records.
In addition, Alaska uses ranked choice voting in general elections, meaning that any remaining confused voters could simply rank both Sullivans in either order.
If none of the four Senate candidates receive at least 50% of the first-choice votes, the lowest finisher will be eliminated and their votes redistributed to voters’ second choices.
The process then repeats until only two candidates are left. Because Peltola and Dan S. Sullivan are expected to receive the majority of the votes, they would be the last two candidates left. A voter who ranks Dan J. Sullivan first and Dan S. Sullivan second would eventually have their vote go to Dan S. Sullivan under that scenario.
